summary: CCC-built 1934 L-4 lookout and WWII Aircraft Warning Service station in the Willamette National Forest, restored and now a seasonal rental.

facts.status_note: Fully restored after rot/insect damage; used in high fire danger periods and rented seasonally.

staffing.status: none (recreation rental; used occasionally in high fire danger)

access.note: High-clearance vehicle recommended; last half mile on foot over steep terrain.

visit.trail_note: Last 2 miles of road are rough gravel/dirt at ~10% grade; last half mile is a walk-in.

events.note: L-4, 14x14 ft house with catwalk, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.
A separate cabin was built north of the lookout and staffed year-round as an Aircraft Warning Service station through WWII.
NHLR says last staffed in the late 1960s; firelookout.com instead says the 1970s, so the exact end year is disputed.
Lookout rebuilt from ground level up due to rot and insect damage; restoration credited to the Pacific Crest Trust Fund per NHLR or the Sand Mountain Society per firelookout.com.

evidence.supports: Built 1934 by CCC, 14x14 L-4 with catwalk; 1942 AWS cabin; last staffed late 1960s; saved by hiking group, restored by Pacific Crest Trust Fund
evidence.quote: The L-4 14'x14' house with catwalk on Gold Butte was constructed in the Willamette National Forest in 1934 by the CCC. Eight years later a cabin was built several hundred feet north of the lookout station and staffed year-around as part of the Aircraft Warning Service in World War II... the lookout -- which was last staffed in the late 1960s -- was saved by a hiking group. The Pacific Crest Trust Fund has raised money and provided volunteers to restore the structure.

evidence.supports: WWII AWS staffing by husband-wife teams reporting aircraft; 3-ft stilts, glass windows, furniture, views, season, access road, half-mile walk-in
evidence.quote: During World War II, the lookout served as part of Aircraft Warning System station in defense of the nation against air attack. It was staffed around the clock, usually by a husband and wife team, who reported all passing aircraft within sight or sound to a central filter center. The lookout stands on 3-foot stilts...

evidence.supports: Built 1934, last used 1970s, Sand Mountain Society rebuilt from ground up due to rot/insect damage, NHLR listed, rental program
evidence.quote: This L-4 ground cab, built in 1934, was last used in the 1970's. The Sand Mountain Society completely restored the structure, literally tearing the cab down to ground level and starting over due to rot and insect damage.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives 'late 1960s'; firelookout.com gives the 1970s. Kept both and flagged the disagreement rather than choosing one.

NHLR credits a hiking group and the Pacific Crest Trust Fund; firelookout.com credits the Sand Mountain Society. Both are named in the story since neither source could be confirmed as more authoritative.

corrections.proposed: Recreation.gov gives 4,618 ft (~1,408 m), vs. NHLR's 4,477 ft (1,365 m) used in the current record
corrections.why: The two agency-linked sources disagree on summit elevation by about 140 feet; not resolved, flagged for editor rather than changed outright.

notes_for_editor: Elevation conflict: brief/NHLR give 4,477 ft (1,365 m), Recreation.gov gives 4,618 ft. Left out of story text since it's a minor figure; see corrections entry. Fact-check 2026-10-04: all three citations re-fetched and verified verbatim against the live sources, including the Recreation.gov Directions section ('last 2 miles of road access are rough gravel and dirt at a 10 percent uphill grade'), which backs the story's 'rough gravel roads' detail though it falls outside the short evidence quote on file. No unsupported claims or citation errors found; no edits needed to the story text.
